title: Food & food-contact materials
subtitle: Diet, packaging, processing and storage
chemical: PFAS, bisphenols, phthalates, pesticides, PCBs — depending on source
summary: Food exposure can reflect environmental contamination, agricultural residues, processing, packaging, storage, or migration from food-contact materials. The relevant chemical, concentration and use conditions must be identified before drawing conclusions.
limitation: A food or package category does not prove the presence of a specific endocrine-active chemical, and detection alone does not establish harmful dose.
example_contexts: Fatty foods that bioaccumulate persistent pollutants
practical_questions: What material is touching the food?
Is the concern migration, residue, or environmental contamination?
Which specific compound was measured?
At what concentration and under what use conditions?

title: Drinking water
subtitle: Source water, treatment and distribution
source: Public water, private wells and contaminated source water
chemical: Selected PFAS and other contaminants depending on location
system: Multiple endocrine and physiological endpoints under study
summary: Drinking-water exposure depends on local contamination, treatment, source-water conditions and the specific chemical measured. PFAS are a prominent example because some are persistent and mobile in water.
limitation: Water risk is concentration- and compound-specific. The presence of a contaminant is not the same as a demonstrated health effect at that measured level.
practical_questions: Was the water actually tested?
Which compound was measured?
What is the concentration?
Is an applicable regulatory or health-based benchmark available?
source_label: U.S. EPA — PFAS in Drinking Water

title: Cookware
subtitle: Surface chemistry, coatings and heating conditions
source: Cooking surfaces, coatings and food-contact materials
route: Potential transfer to food followed by ingestion; some degradation products may be inhaled under extreme conditions
system: Depends on the actual material and compound
summary: Cookware should be evaluated by its material, coating chemistry, physical condition, heating temperature and realistic migration or degradation data. 'Nonstick' is a product property, not a toxicological identity.
limitation: It is inaccurate to treat all cookware or all fluorinated chemistry as equivalent. Polymer coatings, processing aids and small-molecule PFAS are different exposure questions.
chemical_classes: PFAS-related chemistry in some manufacturing contexts
exposure_routes: Inhalation if materials are severely overheated
practical_questions: What is the cooking surface made of?
Is the coating intact?
What temperatures are being used?
Is there migration data for the specific material?

title: Clothing & textiles
subtitle: Fabric treatments, finishes and indoor transfer
source: Apparel, upholstery, carpets and treated textiles
chemical: PFAS, flame retardants, phthalates or other additives depending on product
route: Dermal contact, inhalation or ingestion of transferred dust; indirect environmental exposure
summary: Textiles can contain finishes or additives for stain, water, oil or flame resistance. Exposure depends on the actual treatment, chemical release and contact scenario rather than the textile category alone.
limitation: A label such as 'water resistant' or 'flame resistant' does not identify the chemical formulation. Product-specific composition matters.
practical_questions: Is the product chemically treated?
Does the manufacturer disclose the finish?
Is exposure likely to be dermal, via dust, or mainly environmental?
Is the chemical class known?

title: Plastics
subtitle: Polymer type, additives and use conditions
source: Plastic containers, vinyl, household goods and material additives
chemical: Bisphenols, phthalates and other additives depending on polymer and formulation
route: Ingestion, dermal contact, inhalation or dust ingestion
system: Reproductive, metabolic and other endocrine pathways depending on compound
summary: Plastic is not one chemical. Exposure questions usually concern monomers, plasticizers, stabilizers, colorants or other additives, and whether they migrate or are released under actual use conditions.
limitation: A recycling code or the word 'plastic' cannot by itself establish endocrine activity, exposure magnitude or health risk.
practical_questions: What polymer is it?
Which additives are used?
Is it heated or heavily worn?
Is there direct food or skin contact?

title: Cosmetics & personal care
subtitle: Ingredients, frequency and dermal use
source: Fragrances, lotions, cosmetics and personal-care formulations
chemical: Selected phthalates, parabens and other ingredients depending on formulation
route: Primarily dermal; inhalation or incidental ingestion can also occur
system: Reproductive and other endocrine signaling depending on compound
summary: Personal-care exposure is driven by the ingredient list, formulation, amount used, skin area and frequency. Some ingredients have endocrine-activity research, but products should not be treated as toxicologically interchangeable.
limitation: The presence of an ingredient with endocrine activity in a laboratory system does not by itself establish adverse effects from typical product use.
practical_questions: Which ingredient is the concern?
Is it listed or inferred?
How often is the product used?
What human exposure data exist for that ingredient?

title: Household environment
subtitle: Dust, air, furnishings and building materials
source: Indoor dust, furniture, electronics, flooring and older building materials
chemical: Flame retardants, phthalates, PCBs and other semi-volatile chemicals depending on setting
route: Dust ingestion, inhalation and dermal contact
system: Thyroid, reproductive and developmental pathways depending on compound
summary: Many semi-volatile chemicals can move from products into indoor air and dust. Household exposure therefore links product composition, ventilation, cleaning, age of materials and hand-to-mouth behavior.
limitation: Indoor dust contains complex mixtures. Measuring one chemical does not establish that it caused a particular health outcome.
practical_questions: What material is the likely source?
Is the building older?
Was dust or air actually measured?
Which compound or mixture was detected?
source_label: NIEHS — Indoor Environment and Endocrine Disruptors
